subject: Animation
title: MGM's Tom and Jerry
description: One-minute skill: MGM's Tom and Jerry.

hook.text: In 1940, Hanna and Barbera created a cat-and-mouse cartoon that relied purely on slapstick.

buildup.text: Tom and Jerry had almost no dialogue. The comedy came purely from movement, timing, and pain.

discovery.text: The duo won seven Academy Awards, more than any other animated series in history.

twist.text: MGM shut down its animation department in 1957, thinking cartoons had no future on television.

climax.text: Tom and Jerry outlived the studio's doubt, running on TV for decades after MGM abandoned them.

punchline.text: A silent cat and mouse won more Oscars than most studios.

quiz.question: How many Academy Awards did Tom and Jerry win?
options: Seven, more than any other animated series

details.summary: Tom and Jerry, created by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera at MGM, became one of the most successful cartoon series in history. The cat-and-mouse slapstick featured extraordinary animation quality and won seven Academy Awards between 1943 and 1953.
details.whyItMatters: Tom and Jerry demonstrated that brilliant physical comedy and animation craftsmanship could create timeless entertainment without dialogue. The series also trained the animators who would later create Hanna-Barbera's television empire.
takeaways: Tom and Jerry won seven Academy Awards for Best Animated Short Film
The series featured exceptional animation quality and physical comedy
Creators Hanna and Barbera later revolutionized television animation

faq.question: How many Academy Awards did Tom and Jerry win?
faq.answer: Seven, between 1943 and 1953 — more than any other animated series. The theatrical shorts featured lavish animation, perfectly timed physical comedy, and creative gag construction that made each short a miniature masterwork.

faq.question: How did Tom and Jerry lead to television animation?
faq.answer: When MGM closed its animation department, William Hanna and Joseph Barbera founded their own studio. Using the production skills learned making theatrical shorts, they developed limited animation techniques for television, creating The Flintstones, Scooby-Doo, and dozens of other shows.
